title: Mu'adh ibn Jabal
hook: sent to Yemen and asked how he would judge: by the book, then the sunnah, then his own reasoning (Abu Dawud)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Zayd ibn Thabit, who wrote at the board while the verse was still arriving. Your line was the young scribe.

A man is about to ride south to Yemen, far from Medina, where he will be the one people bring their quarrels to. There will be no running back to ask. Before he goes, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, stops him with a question, the kind a teacher asks just before the exam. How will you judge, when a case comes to you? The man's answer is short, and it comes in three steps. Today: Mu'adh ibn Jabal.
screen: `A RIDE SOUTH TO YEMEN.` → `NO RUNNING BACK TO ASK.` → `HOW WILL YOU JUDGE?`

segments.voice: Abu Dawud records the conversation. How will you judge? By the book of God, Mu'adh says. And if you don't find it in the book of God? Then by the sunnah of the Messenger of God. And if you don't find it in the sunnah, or in the book? Then I will use my own reasoning, Mu'adh says, and I will not fall short. And the Prophet, the report says, struck him on the chest and praised God for guiding the messenger of His Messenger to what pleases the Messenger of God. The book first. Then the example of the Prophet. And only then, when both are silent on the case in front of you, your own careful thinking, done honestly and with effort. Hadith scholars have discussed the strength of this report's chain; some accept it and some question it. Its shape is clear, though, and some readers take a habit from it even outside a courtroom: not jumping straight to one's own opinion. Sahih al-Bukhari adds the advice the Prophet gave Mu'adh and Abu Musa when they set out for Yemen: make things easy, and do not make them hard. Give good news, and do not drive people away. Work together, and do not fall out. A judge with a method, and a gentle way of using it. Book, sunnah, reason.
screen: `FIRST, THE BOOK OF GOD.` · `THEN, THE SUNNAH.` · `THEN, MY OWN REASONING.` · `MAKE THINGS EASY, NOT HARD.` · then, large: `BOOK, SUNNAH, REASON.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one judgment you've made recently, or are about to make, and slow it into steps: what do the facts actually say, what would the wisest person you know do, and only then, what do you think? Notice if the judgment softens or sharpens. If you pray, you can ask for fairness in what you decide.
Ijtihad, striving, the careful reasoning Mu'adh ibn Jabal said he'd use when the book and the sunnah were both silent, and would not fall short on. Today's word.
Your line: book, sunnah, reason. The order matters as much as the answer. Day eight hundred thirty-five, done.

howItsDone: Students of Islamic law learn the hadith of Mu'adh from Sunan Abu Dawud as a picture of how a judge reasons: the Qur'an, then the sunnah, then careful reasoning (ijtihad).

chat.says: How did Mu'adh say he'd judge a case in Yemen?
options: The book of God, then the sunnah, then his own reasoning if both were silent.
By his own reasoning first, checking the book only if people disagreed.
By local custom in Yemen, so people would accept his rulings more easily.
chat.meaning: In Abu Dawud's report: by the book of God, then the sunnah, then I will use my own reasoning and not fall short.

Yemen.meaning: the land to the south where Mu'adh was sent

Abu Musa.meaning: a companion sent to Yemen with Mu'adh

Mu'adh ibn Jabal.meaning: a companion sent to Yemen as a judge
